newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO trade blame for Hebron violence.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO trade blame for Hebron violence.

text.p: Israel and the PLO traded blame for fresh violence in the West Bank powderkeg of Hebron, where Israeli gunfire wounded three Palestinians .
Israel's state-run television showed the army's reaction to a hail of stones thrown at soldiers on Thursday. It filmed uniformed troops kicking detained protesters in the head, back, and groin.
Israeli bullets and Palestinian petrol bombs and stones have peppered the town since a Jewish woman ignited Arab anger by posting placards at the weekend mocking the Prophet Mohammad.
Israel blamed the unrest squarely on the Palestinian Authority and warned the self-rule body to halt the violence or risk a stronger military response.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, holding fast to his government's hardline stance, told reporters the unrest was "organised by the Palestinian Authority and in those cases where it's not organised by the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian police sit back and do nothing to stop this."
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat rejected Netanyhahu's charge. He told reporters "He knows that this is not true."
Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdainah went further, saying Netanyahu had "provoked the Palestinian masses by assaulting their rights, stealing land, and widening settlements".
Israeli-PLO talks collapsed in March, after Netanyahu's government enraged Arabs by breaking ground on a new settlement in East Jerusalem.

Tatyana Suskin, a 26-year-old Jewish woman, was charged on Thursday with illegally posting placards that depicted Prophet Mohammad as a pig on some 20 Hebron storefronts last Friday, and with endangering life by stoning an Arab car on Saturday. The offences carry a 24-year maximum sentence.
In unrest on Wednesday sparked by anger over the posters, troops wounded 37 youths in Hebron and shot dead an Arab teenager in Gaza.
Netanyahu has strongly denounced the placards.

Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai on Thursday met U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk and Egypt's envoy Mohammad Bassiouny. He said he had "asked them to act with all means" to press the PLO to crack down on Hebron violence.
But Egypt, main mediator of the troubled peace process, said it was up to Israel to change its policies if Cairo's efforts to revive the talks were to bear fruit.
Israel's ally Washington, for its part, said both sides were equally responsible for continuing violence in Hebron, where 400 Jews live among 100,000 Arabs.
The State Department condemned the pasting of the posters, calling Suskin "either sick or evil."
The Hebron clashes on Thursday began near the Jewish enclave of Beit Hadassah on the Israeli-held side of the West Bank town, divided since January under a peace deal with the PLO.

When Palestinians began throwing stones at uniformed troops and burning an Israeli flag, undercover soldiers hidden among the crowd began beating and pushing them, holding one in a headlock and dragging another along the ground, witnesses said.
Paramilitary border police then took custody of the detainees, kicking them as they lay doubled over in pain.
The border police said the incident would be probed.
Soldiers then fired at protesters as stone-throwing continued. Hospital officials said the wounded Palestinians, hit by rubber-coated metal bullets, were not seriously hurt.
